title: Projects & Applied Research
Stakeholder Mapping: Voting Patterns for the Fiscal Framework
text:
The Intersection of Data and Economics
As an aspiring economist, I understand that macroeconomic models and fiscal policies do not exist in a vacuum. The approval of a major economic anchor, such as the new Fiscal Framework (PLP 93/2023), relies heavily on institutional predictability and informal alliances.
This project is a core part of my continuous learning journey in quantitative research. It represents my dedication to pushing my technical boundaries, bridging the gap between raw data engineering and advanced political-economic analysis.



1. Data Manipulation and Algebraic Modeling
To map tactical alliances accurately, we must filter out procedural noise and plenary absences. I quickly learned that relying on simple vote counting often misrepresents true party behavior and strategy. To solve this, I constructed relational matrices utilizing the Jaccard Similarity Index.
Mathematically, this models the exact proportion of agreement between any two parliamentarians based on their shared votes:
\[J(A,B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}\]

Technical Note on Data Engineering: Building this pipeline required rigorous data hygiene. When processing the extracted legislative datasets locally, I optimized the ingestion by strictly parsing standard comma delimiters using read_csv() in R. This fine-tuning ensured the structural integrity of the relational matrices before applying any algebraic transformations.



2. Unsupervised Clustering (Louvain Algorithm)
By applying the Louvain algorithm for community detection, the model revealed the invisible behavioral caucuses within the Congress.
The results provided crucial insights for economic risk assessment: the algorithm indicated a pragmatic fragmentation of the “Centrão” into two distinct negotiation masses, directly reflecting the transaction costs and the slicing of parliamentary amendments. Furthermore, it mathematically captured the opposition, highlighting the tactical union of ideological extremes (PL and PSOL) in resistance to the fiscal agenda.


3. Network Metrics and Stakeholder Identification
Using Gephi (ForceAtlas 2) for topological mapping, I extracted the Betweenness Centrality metric for the network.
This calculation successfully identified the parliamentarians acting as strategic articulators—the literal bridges between rival blocs. For public policy forecasting, identifying these decision-makers is vital. Because they control the flow of negotiations and information, they hold the power to unlock or stall the formation of a majority for the country’s economic agenda.

title: Administrative Unilateralism in Latin America
text:
Scaling Up Institutional Analysis
Understanding comparative political requires analyzing institutional rules at scale. Guided by the methodological frameworks established in current academic literature on unilateralism, this project has been a steep but highly rewarding learning curve in processing “text-as-data”.
My role focuses on the backend infrastructure and data intelligence, managing the complexities of standardizing legal structures across Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Colombia, and Paraguay.



1. Web Scraping at Scale (150,000+ Records)
Extracting data from dynamic and often unstable governmental portals requires resilient code. I conceptualized and automated script routines for systematic batch processing.
This involved overcoming pagination barriers, managing server request rates, and bypassing connection instabilities to successfully consolidate a unified database of over 150,000 official normative records.


2. Statistical Programming and Strict Data Validation
Cleaning and modeling large institutional databases requires extreme precision. When validating the data for Argentine legislative relations, for example, I learned the critical importance of strict data alignment. I designed the logic to ensure that legislative texts were only counted in our metrics if they were definitively present in the local text database. Handling these discrepancies natively within the code ensures the integrity of the cross-country analysis.


3. Natural Language Processing (NLP)
To move beyond metadata, I applied NLP techniques to decode the raw content of decrees and official acts—a crucial step for identifying regulatory selectivity.

Pre-processing & Vectorization: Transforming legal jargon into structured data.
Named Entity Recognition (NER): Automatically identifying and categorizing key political and economic actors within the texts.

Learning Note: This project marked a significant step in my technical evolution, bridging the gap between traditional web scraping and advanced computational text analysis for regulatory policy assessment.

title: Budget Gatekeepers: Federal Transfer Network in Brazil
text:
Connecting Public Finance to Political Strategy
As my focus shifts increasingly toward economics and public finance, I constantly seek out complex challenges that force me to expand my quantitative toolkit. This project has been instrumental in that journey, driving me to deepen my knowledge in econometrics to investigate party bargaining power in the distribution of federal resources (Voluntary Transfers of the Union) to Brazilian municipalities.
This research goes beyond mapping; it is a rigorous political-economic analysis of how institutional “gatekeepers” control access to public funds.



1. Data Science and ETL (Panel Data)
Building a robust economic analysis requires pristine data infrastructure. I structured longitudinal panel data spanning from 2011 to 2016, containing thousands of observations.
This complex ETL pipeline integrates: * Budgetary microdata from TransfereGov/Siconv. * Territorial matching between IBGE and TSE datasets via crosswalks. * Automated consumption of the Chamber of Deputies API to capture the true, fluctuating size of parliamentary caucuses.
Learning Note: Designing this architecture taught me how to handle high-dimensional relational data and merge disparate governmental sources without losing observational integrity.


2. Relational Intelligence
I constructed and projected bipartite networks to map the exact flow of public money between municipalities and intermediaries (Ministries and Parliamentarians). By applying Betweenness Centrality calculations, the model successfully identifies the institutional gatekeepers controlling access to the public treasury.


3. Econometric Modeling
To measure the “coalition bonus”—the interactive effect between ministerial control and legislative strength—I estimated multiple regression models (Ordinary Least Squares). This approach allowed me to mathematically quantify the impact of the budgetary decentralization generated by the institutional shock of the Impositive Amendments (EC 86/2015).

title: Francisco Blasco
text:
About me
Welcome to my portfolio. I am an undergraduate student in International Economic Relations at the Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG) and researcher with the Executives, Presidents, and Cabinets Politics (PEX-Network) group, affiliated with the Center for Legislative Studies (CEL-DCP/UFMG).
My work is centered on political-economic analysis and the evaluation of public policies. I build structured datasets and apply quantitative methods to analyze Executive-Legislative dynamics and their impacts on economic development and institutional frameworks.
